items.title: Iran tensions shadow White House state dinner for British royals

featured_image.name: See King Charles, Queen Camilla at Trump's White House dinner

items.description: President Donald Trump and King Charles III celebrated the enduring alliance between their nations at a White House state dinner on Tuesday evening, capping a day of pomp and diplomacy that included the king's rare address to a joint session of Congress. The White House marked the occasion by posting a photo of the two leaders on social media with the caption "TWO KINGS," a move that drew widespread attention.[1][2]

items.title: France unveils roadmap to end all fossil fuel use by 2050

featured_image.name: France outlines ‘first of its kind’ plan to phase out fossil fuels by 2050

items.description: France on Tuesday presented what it called a "first of its kind" national roadmap to phase out coal by 2030, oil by 2045, and natural gas by 2050, laying out a comprehensive timeline for weaning Europe's second-largest economy off fossil fuels entirely.[1][2]

items.title: Asian stocks rise, oil falls after UAE quits OPEC

featured_image.name: UAE leaves OPEC in blow to oil cartel during war on Iran

items.description:
The United Arab Emirates announced on Tuesday that it will leave OPEC and OPEC+ effective May 1, ending nearly six decades of membership in the oil cartel and sending ripples through global energy and equity markets.

Asian stocks mostly advanced on Wednesday despite the upheaval, while oil prices fell as traders assessed the implications of losing one of OPEC's largest producers. The Kospi rose 0.3% in Seoul, Hong Kong's Hang Seng climbed about 1%, and the Shanghai Composite edged up 0.3%, according to the Associated Press. India's Sensex gained 0.4%, while Australia's S&P/ASX 200 dipped 0.3% and Taiwan's Taiex fell 0.6%. Japanese markets were closed for a holiday. Brent crude and U.S. benchmark crude both declined in early Wednesday trading.[1]

items.title: Adelaide researchers map path to turning plastic into hydrogen fuel

featured_image.name: Solar photoreforming turns plastic waste into clean fuel at low temperatures

items.description:
Researchers at Adelaide University have laid out a roadmap for converting plastic waste into hydrogen and other clean fuels using sunlight, advancing a technology they say could address both pollution and energy challenges simultaneously.

The study, published this week in the journal Chem Catalysis, examines how a process known as solar-driven photoreforming uses light-activated materials called photocatalysts to break down plastics at relatively low temperatures, producing hydrogen — a zero-emissions fuel — along with syngas, acetic acid, and even diesel-range hydrocarbons.[1][2]

items.title: EU finds Meta failed to block under-13s from Instagram, Facebook

featured_image.name: EU investigates Meta over Facebook and Instagram child safety

items.description:
The European Commission on Wednesday issued preliminary findings that Meta violated the Digital Services Act by failing to stop children under 13 from using Facebook and Instagram, escalating one of the bloc's most closely watched enforcement cases against a major tech company.

The Commission said Meta had failed to "diligently identify, assess and mitigate the risks of minors under 13 years old accessing their services," despite its own terms and conditions setting 13 as the minimum age for both platforms. If the findings are upheld, Meta could face fines of up to 6% of its global annual revenue.[1][2]

items.title: Europe hit record wildfires and Arctic heatwaves in 2025, new climate report finds

featured_image.name: Satellite imagery captures devastating wildfires across Europe in 2025 |  EUMETSAT

items.description:
Europe endured its second-worst heatwave season on record in 2025, with extreme heat stretching from the Mediterranean to the Arctic Circle and wildfires burning the largest area ever documented, according to the European State of the Climate report released on Tuesday by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).[1][2][3]

The report, drawing on contributions from around 100 scientists, found that at least 95 percent of Europe experienced above-average annual temperatures in 2025, with the United Kingdom, Norway, and Iceland recording their hottest years on record. A three-week heatwave in sub-Arctic Fennoscandia pushed temperatures above 30°C within the Arctic Circle, while southern and eastern Spain endured up to 50 additional days where temperatures felt like 32°C or higher.[4][2][3][1]

items.title: Tropical forest loss fell 36% in 2025, but fires threaten gains

featured_image.name: The year in rainforests 2025: Deforestation fell; the risks did not

items.description:
The world lost 4.3 million hectares of tropical primary rainforest in 2025 — an area roughly the size of Denmark — representing a 36% decline from the record-shattering losses of 2024, according to new data released Wednesday by the World Resources Institute's Global Forest Watch platform.[1][2]

The findings, produced by the University of Maryland's GLAD Lab, show that strong government action can curb deforestation. But researchers warn the drop may reflect fewer fires rather than durable progress, and that loss levels remain about 70% higher than what is needed to meet the 2030 goal of halting deforestation.[2][1]

items.title: King Charles urges unity in rare address to Congress

featured_image.name: Read King Charles' Full Speech to Congress

items.description:
King Charles III addressed a joint session of the U.S. Congress on Tuesday, calling on the two nations to defend their shared democratic values and declaring that "time and again, our two countries have always found ways to come together," in a rare royal speech to American lawmakers that carried unmistakable undertones about the strains testing the transatlantic alliance.[1][2]

The address — only the second by a British monarch before Congress, after Queen Elizabeth II's 1991 speech — came on the second day of a four-day state visit and at a moment of acute tension between Washington and London over the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran and President Donald Trump's sharp criticism of NATO allies.[3][4]

items.title: Ships cross Strait of Hormuz as U.S.-Iran standoff stalls

featured_image.name: First Japan-linked crude tanker braves Hormuz since start of war

items.description:
Four civilian ships passed through the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, including a Japanese supertanker carrying some two million barrels of Saudi crude oil, even as competing U.S. and Iranian blockades continue to choke one of the world's most vital waterways two months into the conflict.[1]

The transits came as the Trump administration weighed a new Iranian proposal to mutually lift restrictions on the strait in exchange for delaying nuclear talks, a deal that appeared unlikely to gain traction in Washington.[2][1]

items.title: Amazon to offer OpenAI models on AWS after Microsoft exclusivity ends

featured_image.name: Microsoft, OpenAI rewrite partnership to eliminate exclusive model ...

items.description:
Microsoft and OpenAI announced on Monday that their partnership has been restructured, ending Microsoft's exclusive license to OpenAI's models and products — a change that immediately opened the door for Amazon to begin distributing OpenAI's technology through its cloud platform.

Hours after the announcement, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy posted on X calling it a "very interesting announcement," adding that the company is "excited to make OpenAI's models available directly to customers on Bedrock in the coming weeks, alongside the upcoming Stateful Runtime Environment."[1][2]

items.title: U.S. Marines board cargo ship in Arabian Sea to enforce Iran blockade

featured_image.name: How US Marines can protect commercial shipping in the Gulf

items.description: U.S. Marines on Tuesday boarded and searched a commercial vessel in the Arabian Sea suspected of attempting to reach Iran in violation of the American naval blockade, the military said, before releasing the ship after confirming it was not headed to an Iranian port.

items.title: Cursor AI agent wiped startup's database in 9 seconds, founder says

featured_image.name: An AI agent allegedly deleted a startup's production database ...

items.description: An AI coding agent wiped a startup's entire production database and all its backups in a single API call lasting nine seconds, leaving car rental businesses scrambling to serve customers with no booking records over the weekend.

items.title: Trump claims Iran in 'state of collapse,' wants Hormuz reopened

featured_image.name: Trump extends Iran ceasefire but continues Hormuz blockade

items.description:
President Donald Trump claimed on Tuesday that Iran has asked the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, portraying Tehran as desperate to end a naval blockade that has choked its economy amid a fragile ceasefire between the two nations.

"Iran has just informed us that they are in a 'State of Collapse.' They want us to 'Open the Hormuz Strait,' as soon as possible, as they try to figure out their leadership situation," Trump posted on Truth Social, adding that he believes Iran will be able to resolve its internal issues.[1][2][3]

items.title: DOJ indicts former FBI director Comey a second time

featured_image.name: Federal judge sets back Justice Department's effort to seek new ...

items.description:
The Department of Justice has indicted former FBI Director James Comey for the second time, CNN reported on Tuesday, citing two sources familiar with the matter. The specific charges in the new indictment have not yet been publicly disclosed.

The move marks an escalation in the Trump administration's legal pursuit of Comey, whose first indictment in September 2025 was dismissed after a federal judge found the prosecutor who brought the case had been unlawfully appointed.

items.title: Japanese supertanker becomes first to exit Gulf since Iran war began

featured_image.name: 1st Japanese crude tanker crosses Hormuz since start of Mideast conflict

items.description: A sanctioned Russian oligarch's superyacht and a Japanese crude oil supertanker have each transited the blockaded Strait of Hormuz in recent days, underscoring cracks in the competing maritime restrictions imposed by the United States and Iran since war broke out in late February.

items.title: Study confirms deep-ocean heat is shifting toward Antarctica

featured_image.name: Trapped subsurface heat may have triggered Antarctica's sudden sea ice loss

items.description:
Warm water lurking deep in the Southern Ocean has been creeping steadily closer to Antarctica over the past two decades, eroding the cold barrier that has long shielded the continent's ice shelves from melting, according to a study published this week in the journal Communications Earth & Environment.[1]

The research, led by the University of Cambridge with collaborators from the Scripps Institution of Oceanography and UCLA, represents the first observational confirmation that a vast body of warm water known as circumpolar deep water has expanded and shifted toward the Antarctic continental shelf. Climate models had long predicted such a migration, but until now scientists lacked the data to confirm it was underway.[2][3]

items.title: Iran war reshapes global energy as renewables shield some nations from price surge

featured_image.name: A timeline of how the Iran war shook oil prices — and what comes next

items.description: The war between the United States, Israel, and Iran has triggered what the International Energy Agency calls the "greatest global energy security challenge in history," reshaping energy flows worldwide as extreme heat compounds the crisis. The disruption is driving record demand for Chinese clean energy exports, pushing fossil fuel-dependent nations like India to their limits, and offering a case study in resilience for renewable-heavy countries like Albania.

items.title: UCLA study finds desert dust traps twice the heat models estimated

featured_image.name: Climate change is altering Saharan dust – and Europe is downwind

items.description:
Airborne desert dust absorbs and retains roughly twice as much of Earth's heat as climate models have calculated, according to new research from UCLA published in Nature Communications.[1][2]

The study, led by UCLA atmospheric scientist Jasper Kok, found that the heat-trapping effect of dust is equal to about 10% of the warming caused by human-emitted carbon dioxide — double the approximately 5% that most climate models currently estimate.[2][1]

items.title: UAE exits OPEC and OPEC+ effective May 1, fracturing oil alliance

featured_image.name: Middle East Newsletter: Saudis, UAE End Dispute That Rocked OPEC

items.description:
The United Arab Emirates announced on Tuesday that it is withdrawing from both OPEC and OPEC+, effective May 1, dealing a severe blow to the oil-producing alliance and its de facto leader, Saudi Arabia, at a time when the Iran war has already caused the largest supply disruption in the history of global oil markets.[1][2]

The departure of the UAE — a founding member of OPEC since 1967, four years before the nation's own founding — marks the most consequential defection from the cartel in decades and could weaken an organization that has long sought to project unity despite internal rifts over production quotas and geopolitics.[2][1]

items.title: Osaka researchers demo wireless EEG powered by body heat alone

featured_image.name: No batteries, just body heat: Demonstrating the potential of battery-free  sensing

items.description: Researchers at the University of Osaka have developed a wireless brainwave monitoring system that runs entirely on the temperature difference between the human body and surrounding air, eliminating the need for batteries or any external power source. The work, published in the Proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Consumer Electronics, was demonstrated live at Expo 2025 in Osaka, Japan.[1][2]
